headline: Paul Brennan sees Australian housing market slowing as rate rises work through with a lag, with sellers becoming more realistic on price expectations
reasoning: Brennan observes that while weekly auction clearance rates have shown some improvement, this reflects sellers becoming more realistic about price expectations rather than a genuine demand recovery. He views the housing market slowdown as consistent with monetary policy working through with a lag. The pattern of some properties selling at auction while others fail due to a gap between vendor and buyer price expectations is seen as evidence that rate rises are achieving their intended effect of cooling the housing market.
quote: It does seem to be, you know, there has been a little bit of better news in terms of their weekly clearance rates, auction clearance rates. Um, but, you know, that's, I think, reflecting the fact that, that sellers are now more realistic in terms of price expectations. So I think it sort of all consistent with the idea that, you know, these interest rate rises, they do work with a lag and, you know, it is slowing the the economy and the housing market particularly.

headline: Paul Brennan flags consumer confidence still below average despite a modest uptick, pointing to continued consumer spending slowdown ahead
reasoning: While consumer confidence has risen slightly, Brennan notes there are still net more pessimists than optimists, which he views as consistent with consumer spending continuing to slow. He expects this to show up in hard spending data over the next couple of months. The RBA's continued jawboning about no imminent rate relief is seen as deliberately keeping a lid on consumer optimism and spending, reinforcing the macro tightening picture.
quote: We've still got, you know, net terms more pessimists than, than optimists. And I think those figures are consistent with consumer spending slowing. Um, so that's what we'll be watching for Juliet over the next couple of months, is that we actually see that, uh, you know, in the hard data. But the softer data, you know, these sentiment measures are telling us that, um, you know, yes, consumers aren't going to sort of, you know, totally pessimistic, but equally, you know, they're they're still, you know, sort of are worried about things such as, you know, the the prospect of higher interest rates. And that's what the RBA is trying to sort of keep a lid on, keep keeping reminding people that, you know, there's no interest rate relief anytime soon.

headline: Paul Brennan (Suncorp) expects RBA to remain on hold for rest of year as economy slows, with July unemployment rise to 4.5% supporting that base case
reasoning: Paul Brennan notes that the rise in unemployment from 4.4% to 4.5% and a sharp fall in hours worked are consistent with the economy slowing, which is what the RBA has signalled is needed to return inflation to the 2.5% target. His base case is that the RBA will remain on hold for the remainder of the year, with these labour market figures supporting that view. He also points to three consecutive rate rises earlier in the year having had a meaningful shock effect on consumer behaviour and the housing market. Consumer confidence has ticked up but remains below average, with more pessimists than optimists, which is consistent with consumer spending slowing. He expects the hard spending data over the next couple of months to confirm what the softer sentiment data is already indicating.
quote: My base case is that that they will remain on hold. Um, and these figures today, I think support that. Absolutely. But you touched there on what Deputy Governor Houser mentioned yesterday. Um, do you see that speech in conjunction with what we heard from the governor last week as somewhat potentially of jaw boning here? Definitely jaw boning. And I think it does work because doing the the three interest rate rises back to back early in the year I think did really have a shock effect, did really make people sit up and notice that the RBA is serious.

headline: Paul Brennan expects at least one more Fed rate hike before year-end given US inflation remains above target
reasoning: Brennan acknowledges mixed signals from the Fed Chair but believes the US economy remains healthy and inflation is well above target. He thinks the market is right to price in at least one more rate rise from the Fed before year-end. He notes uncertainty around the Fed's reaction function to inflation as a key risk to this view.
quote: I think you know the US economy still looks pretty healthy. And you know inflation like in Australia is well above their target. So I think, you know, the market is is right to be sort of pricing at least one more interest rate rise, I think before the end of the year from the fed.
episode_title: Why Paul sees an RBA pause, not pivot

headline: Sees at least one more Fed rate hike likely, but flags uncertainty over Powell's inflation commitment
reasoning: Brennan notes two competing interpretations of recent Fed messaging: one view is that Powell deliberately steered markets toward higher bond yields to do the Fed's tightening work for it, which is especially important in the US where mortgages are priced off long-term rates rather than the short-term cash rate. The contrary view is that uncertainty about Powell's reaction function and commitment to bringing inflation down explains the yield move, suggesting mixed messages rather than masterful communication. Brennan holds an open mind but concludes that with the US economy still healthy and inflation well above target, the market is right to price at least one more rate hike before year-end.
quote: Like it's really hard to judge because, you know, there's two schools of thought on this. One is that, you know, it was that he's actually a master in terms of steering the market towards doing a lot of the work for the fed that is, you know, underwriting a move up in bond yields. And in the US that's really important because unlike Australia, where, you know, the economy is very sensitive to short term interest rates, i.e. the RBA cash rate in the US, you know, mortgages are set off longer term interest rates. So that's the sort of the view that, you know, yes, he had that effect. You know the yields went up. But the contrary view of course is that well, maybe he's more of an apprentice rather than a master because you know, the why the bond yields rose in the US was because they're so uncertain about, you know, what is his reaction function to dealing with inflation. You know, how committed is he to getting inflation actually down. So he gave a bit. Mixed messages there. So I'm sort of got an open mind on that. But you know for the time being I think you know the US economy still looks pretty healthy. And you know inflation like in Australia is well above their target. So I think, you know, the market is is right to be sort of pricing at least one more interest rate rise, I think before the end of the year.
episode_title: Why Paul sees an RBA pause, not pivot

headline: Paul Brennan sees RBA on hold after three hikes, with unemployment needing to drift higher before further tightening
reasoning: After three successive rate hikes, Brennan believes the RBA is now in a wait-and-see mode to assess how monetary tightening flows through the economy given the well-known long and variable lag. He notes the RBA will likely revise its forecasts toward a slightly higher unemployment rate and slightly lower inflation, which supports the case for a pause. Underlying inflation at 3.6% remains well above the 2.5% midpoint target, and the supply side is not providing relief, meaning demand must slow further. Brennan thinks unemployment may need to drift a little higher before the RBA is confident it has done enough. He also flags that the pass-through of lower house prices to actual spending data has not yet fully materialised, which should add further drag.
quote: I think having done three interest rate rises in quick succession, they're now sort of watching to see exactly how the economy, sort of how those interest rate rises work through the economy. Because, Juliette, we know that interest rates work with a so-called long and variable lag. So it's going to take, I think, a bit of time for them, for the RBA to judge whether they've done enough. I think they probably have. Um, and, you know, in terms of next week, I think it's, you know, the key things will be that on their forecasts for the economy, they're going to have to sort of probably put in a slightly higher outlook for the unemployment rate and slightly lower for inflation. So that also, I think, supports the idea, Juliet, that they're on hold for the time being.
episode_title: Why Paul sees an RBA pause, not pivot

headline: Paul Brennan warns Australian household spending resilience may fade as lower house prices flow through with a lag
reasoning: Brennan notes that spending data through June has shown surprising household resilience, but attributes this partly to the lagged effect of rate hikes not yet fully filtering through. He highlights that lower house prices are already weighing on confidence and expects this to show up in actual spending numbers with a delay. He also points to EV-related motor vehicle spending as a current area of strength supporting imports. Overall, he sees several drags accumulating that should slow spending from here, particularly as the housing market weakness feeds into consumer behaviour.
quote: I think it's sort of partly Juliet because of the lags, you know, that we're still seeing the flow through of the interest rate rises. Obviously one to watch is, you know, what's happening in the housing market with lower house prices. That's I've adding to sort of, I think lower levels of confidence. So people may be sort of that's still really yet to be reflected, I think in the, the actual spending numbers in the economy, because we've only got up to June and we're really only now starting to see the the effects of the lower house prices on the, on on spending, I suspect.
episode_title: Why Paul sees an RBA pause, not pivot

headline: Expects US nonfarm payrolls to show ~80k job gain with unemployment steady at 4.2%, consistent with a resilient economy
reasoning: Brennan notes the market is looking for a sub-100k, around 80,000 increase in payrolls with the unemployment rate staying stable at around 4.2%. This would indicate the US economy remains in a holding pattern — still resilient and robust. He links this resilience to strong US corporate earnings season which has supported equity markets.
quote: I think the market is sort of looking for another reasonable number, you know, a sub 100, about 80,000 increase in employment and payrolls. But for the unemployment rate to stay stable at around 4.2%. So that again sort of says, you know, the economy's probably in this sort of holding pattern where it's still quite resilient and robust. And that's been reflected, of course, Gilead in reporting season in the US, where, you know, company reports have been shooting the lights out broadly and that's been supporting, you know, the equity market.
episode_title: Why Paul sees an RBA pause, not pivot

headline: Suncorp's Paul Brennan expects RBA to keep rates on hold, with no near-term trigger for hikes
reasoning: Brennan notes that despite a surprisingly strong headline employment figure of 76,000 (vs 15,000 expected), the unemployment rate held steady at 4.4% and hours worked rose only marginally, suggesting the economy is gradually slowing under the weight of previous rate rises. Wage growth has also slowed, and inflation, while sticky above the 2.5% midpoint target, does not appear to be moving higher in underlying terms. The softening housing market adds to the case for holding. He acknowledges some market pricing of a hike risk before year-end but does not see a real trigger for the RBA to raise rates in the short term.
quote: I think, you know they just sort of will continue to sort of leave interest rates where they are. No, really, I don't think there's any real sort of trigger for them to raise interest rates in the short term at least... I think that's why I think, you know, there sort of will be leaving interest rates on hold for the time being. There is that risk though. And we look at market pricing. The market is saying that there's sort of you know, there is a reasonably high risk that the RBA could raise interest rates before the end of the year. So it really is going to depend on to what extent does the economy sort of continue to sort of soften and whether that helps to keep inflation, you know, from rising further.
episode_title: Jobs jump, but will the RBA stay put?

headline: Paul Brennan expects AUD to gradually appreciate as USD peaks, with NZD also rising against AUD on RBNZ hawkishness
reasoning: Brennan has been of the view for some time that the USD is peaking around current levels and that the Australian dollar will gradually appreciate. He also highlights that the New Zealand dollar has strengthened roughly 2% off its recent lows, driven by a shift to a more hawkish RBNZ outlook, and currency experts he follows expect further NZD appreciation against the AUD.
quote: I've been sort of thinking for a while that, you know, that the US dollar was sort of peaking around these sort of levels and that we would see the Australian dollar gradually appreciate. Um, the other one, of course, that's of interest for us is the New Zealand dollar. And you know, what's been happening there is, is because the RBNZ has shifted to a sort of a much more hawkish sort of outlook that's been supportive of the New Zealand dollar. So you know, currently the New Zealand dollar has risen about 2% off its low from last last month. And most of the sort of the currency experts that I plug into, they're basically saying that we'll continue to see a further rise in the New Zealand dollar against the Australian dollar.
episode_title: Jobs jump, but will the RBA stay put?

headline: Rising oil prices a headwind for Australian consumer discretionary income but unlikely to fully pass through to CPI
reasoning: Brennan observes that consumer confidence is low and rising oil prices will further squeeze discretionary income, helping keep a lid on demand. However, he draws on the experience from the earlier phase of the war-related oil shock, where higher oil prices did not fully pass through into consumer prices, and expects a similar outcome this time around.
quote: Confidence is low. You know, the fact that the oil price is rising again isn't going to be helpful because that's going to feed into discretionary income. And so that'll I think help to keep a lid on things. I guess the worry is though that the higher oil price then feeds into ongoing inflation. But the evidence from the first round of the shock, when we only had the the height of the war, the first phase of the war earlier this year was that we didn't see the full impact of the higher oil prices being passed through into consumer prices. So I suspect that will be a sort of similar story this time around.
episode_title: Jobs jump, but will the RBA stay put?

headline: Brennan urges caution on AI labour market conclusions, noting it is too early to judge impacts despite some early signs of slower clerical hiring
reasoning: The Australian federal government released a broadly positive report finding no macro evidence of AI undercutting the labour market, with employment for under-25s actually growing faster than for older cohorts. However, clerical positions are showing slower employment growth relative to others. Brennan cautions that given how early we are in this technology shock, definitive conclusions cannot be drawn. He notes US data showing a sharp slowdown in college graduate hiring as a signal worth watching, and argues judgment should be withheld for now.
quote: My only comment would be it's just so early in the in, in this sort of, you know, this incredible technology shock to really sort of make definitive conclusions about how it's going to play out. And we all really, you know, we really don't know at this stage. You know, there's been talk in the US that, you know, hiring of college graduates has sort of has, has slowed quite dramatically. So you know, something, you know, that's really uncertain.
episode_title: Rate cuts? Paul says not so fast

headline: Australian consumer and business confidence remain low amid RBA hold messaging, federal budget uncertainty, and AI job concerns, though spending is slowing but not stopping
reasoning: Brennan notes that consumer and business confidence are both depressed, weighed down by multiple factors including the federal budget adding uncertainty, the RBA's warning that it may need to tighten further, and broader concerns around AI's impact on employment. Real-time consumer spending measures show a slowing pace but not an outright contraction. The winter seasonal effect is also cited as a modest headwind to confidence.
quote: Bottom line is that confidence is low. Business confidence is also low as well. Uh, you know, I think the federal budget added to a fair bit of uncertainty in a number of areas as well. Probably didn't help a lot. But, you know, the message and the message from the RBA, even though I think they are on hold for an extended period now, you know, the message is one of, you know, that they're warning that they may have to go back again and tighten further. So that's weighing on confidence as well. We're seeing it in some of the real time measures of consumer actual spending. You know that it's slowed but it's not stopping.

headline: Suncorp's Paul Brennan expects RBA on hold for the rest of 2025, sees rates at around neutral to slightly restrictive
reasoning: Brennan argues Australia is in a different position to New Zealand, where rates were at exceptionally low levels and are now being hiked back toward neutral. Australia's cash rate at 4.35% is already around neutral or slightly restrictive. Despite the RBA's hawkish messaging warning of possible further tightening, Brennan expects the RBA to remain on hold for the rest of the year, consistent with its historically patient approach to navigating the difficult trade-off between a persistent supply-side shock weighing on growth while also adding to inflation.
quote: I think, you know, when we look back at the how the RBA has acted, they've been sort of relatively patient, you know, to sort of see this sort of dilemma resolved. So my guess is that, you know, we're sort of we're on hold for, for probably for the rest of this year from the RBA.
episode_title: Rate cuts? Paul says not so fast

headline: RBNZ embarking on ~100bp tightening cycle from 2.5% toward 3.25%, with markets now pricing ~90% chance of September hike
reasoning: The RBNZ has started a tightening journey from exceptionally low levels with guidance pointing to rates reaching around 3.25%, implying roughly 100 basis points of hikes. Markets have become increasingly hawkish following the meeting, with the probability of a September hike moving from around 70% to nearly 90%. Brennan flags the key uncertainty is whether the New Zealand economy picks up sufficiently to warrant the pace markets are pricing, given the unemployment rate is still around 5.5%.
quote: After the meeting it was talking about the market was pricing about a 70% chance that the next meeting at the beginning of September would see a hike. Now this morning when I checked it it was nearly 90% probability. So markets really sort of warmed up to the idea that, you know, the RBNZ is going to get on their bike and move faster than what their guidance is, but it really is going to depend on just, you know, whether the economy does really sort of start to pick up a lot.
episode_title: Rate cuts? Paul says not so fast

headline: AUD near 70c helping keep a lid on import prices, limiting inflation upside in Australia
reasoning: Paul Brennan notes that the Australian dollar around US$0.70 is still relatively strong and is helping contain import price inflation. He also observes that even during periods of elevated oil prices, there was limited pass-through into final consumer prices, which is an encouraging sign that inflation is unlikely to get out of control in a way that would force the RBA to tighten again.
quote: Sort of at $0.70, it's still helping to keep a lid on import prices. So that's that's helpful for inflation. Um, you know obviously a lot will depend on how, as you mentioned earlier, Juliet around the Gulf and, you know, the the renewed hostilities there and how that affects the oil price. But what I think the big picture there was that what we saw, even when oil prices were really elevated, what we saw was that there wasn't a lot of pass through of those higher oil prices into final consumer prices. So that's also, I think, a sort of an encouraging sign around, you know, that inflation isn't isn't going to get out of control in a way which would require the RBA to tighten again.
